title: The Teenager at the Table
subtitle: Six sessions for parents moving from controlling a child to discipling a young adult
summary: Somewhere around thirteen the job changes and nobody tells you. The child who used to ask you everything goes quiet, and the temptation is to tighten your grip right when God is asking you to loosen it. This study is six sessions for the parents, not the teenager. It is about the aim being a faith they own rather than a child who obeys, about doubt being a question and not a rebellion, about a borrowed faith that has to become theirs before it can carry them, about identity in a world that keeps a scoreboard, about staying in the room when they pull away, and about blessing the young adult you are already sending. The teenager is not the project here. You are.
setting: A table for the parents first. The teenager is not the project. The parents are the ones being discipled here.
forWho: Parents of tweens and teens, and any adult discipling a teenager, especially the parent watching a once eager child go quiet.
rhythm: Six sessions for the parents, best done by two parents together or a few parents in the same season, not lectured at the teen.
leaderNote: The great temptation with teenagers is to tighten control just as God is asking us to loosen it. The goal was never a compliant child. It was an owned faith. Keep pointing parents from managing behavior to staying in relationship, and from a borrowed faith to the day their child meets God without them. Move slow. Every parent at this table is a little afraid, and most of them think they are the only one. Say the quiet part out loud and watch the room exhale.

sessions.title: From Control to Discipleship
sessions.bigIdea: The aim was never a child who obeys. It was a faith they own. Proverbs asks us to train up a child in the way he should go, and Deuteronomy locates that training in the daily talk of a house, which means the goal is a grown person who still walks the way when we are no longer standing over them.
sessions.open: Think back to when this child was small and did what you said. Name one thing that was easier then, and one thing you did not yet understand about the job.
sessions.read: Read Proverbs 22:6. Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it. Notice the horizon of the verse is not next week but when he is old. Then read Deuteronomy 6:6-7. And these words that I command you today shall be on your heart. You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise.
observe: Proverbs points at when he is old, not while he is young. What does that long horizon do to the way we measure whether parenting is working right now.
In Deuteronomy the words are on the parents heart first, and the teaching happens in ordinary talk, not a lecture. What is the difference between talking with a teenager and talking at one.
talk: Control gets you behavior for as long as you are in the room. Discipleship is after something you cannot force, a faith they choose when you are not watching. Be honest at this table, which one have you actually been aiming at this year.
A compliant teenager can look like success and be hiding. Have you ever mistaken quiet for godly, or a rule kept for a heart changed. What did that cost you or someone you know.
The way he should go is his way, the person God is making, not a copy of us. Where are you trying to raise the child you pictured instead of the one you were given.
sessions.practice: This week catch yourself once about to issue a command and turn it into a question instead. Not to be soft, but to find out what they actually think. Then close your mouth and let the silence do its work.
sessions.send: You are not raising a child who obeys. You are discipling an adult who will one day walk the way without you in the room.
sessions.passItOn: Find one other parent in this season and tell them the shift you are trying to make, from control to discipleship. Ask them where they see you still gripping. A parent who names it out loud to another parent is harder to fool.

sessions.title: When They Start to Doubt
sessions.bigIdea: Doubt is not the opposite of faith and it is not rebellion. A father in Mark cries out that he believes and asks help with his unbelief in the same breath, and Jesus does not scold him. The home has to be the safest place a teenager can bring a hard question, because if it is not, they will take the question somewhere else.
sessions.open: When you were young, was there a question about God you were afraid to ask out loud. Who could you have asked, and what happened to the question when you had no one.
sessions.read: Read Mark 9:24. Immediately the father of the child cried out and said, I believe, help my unbelief. This is a man asking Jesus to heal his son, and his faith and his doubt are living in the same sentence. Then read 1 Peter 3:15. But in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you, yet do it with gentleness and respect.
observe: The father says I believe and help my unbelief in one breath, and Jesus still heals the boy. What does that tell you about how much certainty God requires before he moves.
Peter says give a reason with gentleness and respect. Who usually gets the least gentleness and respect from us, the stranger who asks or the teenager under our own roof.
talk: When a teenager says maybe none of this is true, the body reacts before the heart does. What is your first instinct, to argue, to panic, to fix it fast. What is that instinct really protecting.

There is a difference between a teenager who is done and a teenager who is honest for the first time. We tend to hear rebellion when we are hearing courage. Where might you have punished a question you should have thanked them for.
If your child could ask you anything about God with no flinch and no lecture, they would ask you first instead of a screen at midnight. What would have to change at your table for that to be true.
sessions.practice: This week, when a doubt or a hard question comes, resist the answer for a moment and say tell me more first. If you do not know, say I do not know, let us find out together. You are teaching them that faith can hold a question without breaking.
sessions.send: Doubt is not the end of faith. It is often faith trying to become theirs. Be the safe place, or someone else will be.
sessions.passItOn: Tell one other parent about a question your teenager asked that scared you, and how you tried to stay in the room instead of shutting it down. Most parents think a doubting kid means they failed. Free one of them from that lie this week.

sessions.title: Their Faith, Not Yours
sessions.bigIdea: A borrowed faith cannot carry an adult. The Samaritans told the woman they no longer believed because of her word, for they had heard for themselves. There comes a point where your child has to taste and see that the Lord is good on their own tongue, not just take your word that the meal was fine.
sessions.open: Whose faith did you inherit growing up, if anyone's. Was there a moment it stopped being theirs and started being yours, or are you still waiting on that moment.
sessions.read: Read Psalm 34:8. Oh, taste and see that the LORD is good. Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him. The word is taste, something you have to do with your own mouth. Then read John 4:42, where the townspeople say to the woman, It is no longer because of what you said that we believe, for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is indeed the Savior of the world.
observe: The psalm says taste and see, not hear about and agree. What is the difference between believing a thing is true and having tasted it.
The Samaritans move from because of her word to we have heard for ourselves. What happened in between, and why does that shift matter for a teenager raised in church.
talk: A faith handed down can look identical to a faith owned, right up until pressure comes and one of them buckles. How would you even tell the difference in your own child, and how would you tell it in yourself.

We are often afraid to let a teenager question the faith because we are afraid of what they might conclude. But a faith that cannot survive their honest tasting was never going to carry them anyway. What are you actually afraid of here.
Your job was never to install your faith in them like a program. It was to put the meal in front of them and let them taste. Where are you still trying to swallow it for them.
sessions.practice: This week, instead of telling your teenager what to believe about one thing, ask them what they actually think and why, and then listen without correcting for the length of the whole answer. You are inviting them to taste, not spoon feeding them your conclusion.
sessions.send: You cannot taste the meal for them. You can only keep setting the good food in front of them and pray they pick up the fork.
sessions.passItOn: Ask another parent this: is your kid's faith theirs yet, or still yours. Sit in that question together without rushing to reassure each other. The parents who ask it honestly are the ones who stop performing certainty at their kids.

sessions.title: Identity in an Age of Performance
sessions.bigIdea: Adolescence keeps a scoreboard, grades and follows and bodies and rank, and it tells a teenager they are the sum of the numbers. Paul says the life he now lives he lives by the Son of God who loved him, and the psalm says they were knit together before they had done anything. Their name was written before the first score was tallied.
sessions.open: Name a scoreboard you were measured by as a teenager, spoken or unspoken. Do you still hear it. What did chasing that number cost you.
sessions.read: Read Galatians 2:20. I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me. Then read Psalm 139:13-16. For you formed my inward parts, you knitted me together in my mother's womb. I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. In your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me, when as yet there was none of them.
observe: Paul locates his life in who loved me and gave himself for me, not in what he achieved. Where does he put the weight of his identity, and where does the world tell a teenager to put it.
The psalm says God knit them together and wrote their days before any of them existed, which means before any performance. What does it do to a scoreboard when the verdict came first.
talk: Our teenagers are being told hourly that they are their numbers. But be honest, whose scoreboard did they learn to read at home. What do we celebrate loudest in our house, and what does that teach them they are worth.

There is a difference between good job and I love you and none of this changes that. A performance blessing and an identity blessing sound similar and land completely differently. Which one does your child hear from you more.

Paul says the old self was crucified and a new life is lived by the One who loved him. For a kid drowning in comparison, what would it actually feel like to know the verdict is already in and it is not based on the score.
sessions.practice: This week say one thing to your teenager that has nothing to do with their performance, no grade, no game, no achievement attached. Tell them who they are to you and to God, full stop. Then notice how strange it feels to say it, and ask yourself why.
sessions.send: Their name was written before the first score was ever tallied. Say it to them until it drowns out the scoreboard.
sessions.passItOn: Ask another parent what scoreboard they think their kid is trying to win, and confess the one you have quietly been holding over your own. Naming the family scoreboard to another parent is the first step to taking it down.

sessions.title: Staying in Relationship When They Pull Away
sessions.bigIdea: The father in Luke did not chase the son down the road or lecture him at the gate. He watched, he ran, he embraced. Paul says he shared not only the gospel but his own self, because they had become dear. The pulling away is not the end of the relationship. It is the season that most needs you to keep the door open and your mouth mostly shut.
sessions.open: Think of a time someone kept the door open for you when you were pulling away from them. What did they do, and what did they not do. What made it possible to come back.
sessions.read: Read Luke 15:20. And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him. The father was watching the road, which means he had been watching a long time. Then read 1 Thessalonians 2:8. So, being affectionately desirous of you, we were ready to share with you not only the gospel of God but also our own selves, because you had become very dear to us.
observe: The father runs and embraces before the son gets his speech out. What did the father not do first, and what does that restraint tell you.
Paul says he shared his own self, not only the message. What is the difference between handing a teenager the truth and handing them yourself.
talk: When a teenager pulls away, the lecture feels like doing something and the presence feels like doing nothing. But which one actually keeps them near. Where do you reach for words when what they need is you in the room saying little.

The father in the story had clearly been watching the road for a long time, which means he chose the long game over being right. What would playing the long game cost you with your kid right now, and what are you afraid you would lose.

Sharing your own self means letting them see you, your failures, your doubts, your need for grace, not just your instruction. Where have you kept yourself hidden behind the role of parent, and what might open if you let them see the person.
sessions.practice: This week choose presence over a lecture at least once. Sit with them, drive them somewhere, do the thing they like with no agenda and no teaching moment forced into it. Keep the door open and let them find you easy to be near.
sessions.send: You cannot lecture a pulling child back. You can only keep watching the road and be the kind of parent who is easy to come home to.
sessions.passItOn: Tell one other parent about the door you are keeping open, and ask them to tell you if they ever see you slam it shut with words. Parents in this season need someone to remind them the long game is the only game.

sessions.title: Blessing the Young Adult You Are Sending
sessions.bigIdea: God gave Israel exact words to put on their people, the Lord bless you and keep you. Hannah gave the son she had prayed for back to the Lord, saying he is lent to the Lord. The whole point of the raising was the sending. A young adult should leave your house knowing what you see in them and Who they belong to, said out loud, so they can carry it out the door.
sessions.open: What is a sentence you wish a parent had spoken over you as you left home. Did you leave knowing what they saw in you, or did you have to guess for years.
sessions.read: Read Numbers 6:24-26. The LORD bless you and keep you. The LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you. The LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace. Then read 1 Samuel 1:27-28, where Hannah says, For this child I prayed, and the LORD has granted me my petition that I made to him. Therefore I have lent him to the LORD. As long as he lives, he is lent to the LORD.
observe: In Numbers the blessing puts God's face and God's name on the person, not the parents approval. Where does the blessing get its weight from.
Hannah calls the child lent to the LORD, given back to the One who gave him. What does it change in a parent to hold a child as lent rather than owned.
talk: Many of us left home never once hearing a parent say plainly what they saw in us or Who we belonged to, and some of us are still waiting. What did that silence cost, and what would it mean to be the parent who ends it.

Hannah gave Samuel back to the Lord on purpose, out loud. Every parent gives their child up eventually, but most do it by accident and with clenched hands. What is the difference between a child who slips away and a young adult who is sent with a blessing.

A blessing over a leaving young adult is not a wish that they succeed. It is a naming of who they are and Whose they are, spoken before you know how the story turns out. What words would you want in their ears the day they walk out your door for good.
sessions.practice: Before this study is cold, speak a blessing over your teenager out loud, by name, hand on their shoulder if they will let you. Use Numbers 6 or your own plain words. Tell them what you see in them and remind them Whose they are. Do it before you lose your nerve.
sessions.send: You raised them to send them. Put the words in their ears now, while they are still at your table, so they carry them out the door.
sessions.passItOn: Tell one other parent what happened when you blessed your young adult out loud, and dare them to do the same before their own child leaves. Most houses go silent at the door. Be the parent who tells another parent it does not have to.
